https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c36l.text: Image source, Ritzau Scanpix/Bo Amstrup via REUTERS By Mallory Moench Published 4 hours ago King Harald V of Norway's health has worsened, the palace has said, as he remains in hospital receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his bloodstream. The monarch has responded to treatment despite the deterioration in his condition, according to the palace, but he will remain at Oslo University Hospital, Rikshospitalet, and on leave from royal duties until further notice. The 89-year-old, who has been on the throne since 1991, was admitted to hospital and put on sick leave a week ago. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, 53, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave. King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia. It causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath. In April 2024, Norway's royal household said that King Harald would make a "permanent reduction" to his public engagements "out of consideration for his age". That year, the king had been fitted with a pacemaker after falling ill on holiday in Malaysia. The Norwegian royal family has already faced a challenging year in 2026. Crown Prince Haakon's wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, received a lung transplant in June after she had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis in 2018. The transplant came two days after Mette-Marit's son Marius Borg HÃ¸iby was sentenced to four years in prison after being convicted of two counts of rape. He had denied the most serious charges and his lawyers said he would appeal the sentence. HÃ¸iby, 29, was four when his mother married Crown Prince Haakon and is not himself a royal figure. Also earlier in the year, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later apologised to Norway's king and queen for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/01/bkk-.text: Menü Kereső Új vezérigazgatót kapott a BKK Belföld Bodor Ádám a Mol Bubi új generációjának bemutatóján Budapesten 2026. augusztus 3-án – Fotó: Kovács Márton / MTI Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Szeptember 1-től Bodor Ádám korábbi mobilitási vezérigazgató-helyettes veszi át a Budapesti Közlekedési Központ (BKK) irányítását – közölte a cég kedden. Válóczi István vezérigazgató-helyettesként koordinálja a beruházásokat a továbbiakban, emellett tovább dolgozik a Budapest Közút Zrt.-nél mérnökigazgatóként. Azzal érvelnek, hogy mivel sok uniós forrásból sok fejlesztés fog megvalósulni Budapesten, a cégvezetés hatékonyságáért nevezte ki Karácsony Gergely Bodor Ádámot vezérigazgatónak. Bodor 2020 végén aktív és mikromobilitásért felelős szakértőként csatlakozott a BKK-hoz, majd 2021 áprilisától a Mobilitásfejlesztés Igazgatóságot vezette – írják róla. 2025 áprilisa óta mobilitási vezérigazgató-helyettesként látta el feladatait, majd a BKK igazgatósági elnökévé választották. A BKK előtt más helyeken szintén felügyelte az EU-s források hatékony elköltését, ipari parkban vagy épp a BME Területfejlesztési Kutatási Központjában. A Gyurcsány-kormány idején, 2005–09 között a Gazdasági és Közlekedési Minisztériumban miniszteri biztosként Magyarország első országos kerékpáros programját készítette elő, majd koordinálta megvalósítását. 2010-től 2019-ig az Európai Kerékpáros Szövetség igazgatója volt Brüsszelben, és részt vett a Nemzeti Aktívturisztikai és Kerékpáros stratégia kidolgozásában is. Válócziról azt írják, pályafutását 25 éve a Canor International Kft. projektmenedzsment cégnél kezdte, itt több magas- és mélyépítési beruházás műszaki lebonyolítását, műszaki ellenőrzését végezte. Dolgozott a 4-es metró és az új tévészékház építésén, majd 2013-ban került a Budapest Közúthoz, aminek 2016-ban lett az igazgatóhelyettese, 2018-ban pedig az igazgatója. https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32568.text: Four hundred years ago, the people of a small village in north-central Poland buried a teenage girl with a triangular iron padlock fastened to her toe. That was not enough. Before her body finished decomposing, they opened her grave and laid a curved iron sickle across her throat. And now, a peer-reviewed multidisciplinary study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports has revealed they may have done something else as well — pushed a copper-containing object deep into her mouth or nasal passage around the time of her death. It is the first time in the published archaeological literature that all three measures have been documented in a single burial, and it tells the story of a community so frightened of one young woman that their fear kept escalating long after she was in the ground.The woman — known today by the affectionate nickname Zosia — was the occupant of Grave 75 at an unmarked cemetery near the village of Pień in Poland's Kuyavian-Pomeranian region. The study, led by Professor Dariusz Poliński of the Institute of Archaeology at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, draws on ancient DNA sequencing, radiocarbon dating, stable-isotope analysis, elemental composition mapping (SEM-EDS and MAXRF), and a previous 3D facial reconstruction to build the most complete portrait yet of who she was and why her community was so afraid of her.The research was published on July 30, 2026. Within weeks, it had attracted coverage from CNN, New Atlas, Popular Science, Heritage Daily, and news outlets across multiple continents — a measure of how powerfully the story lands at the intersection of science and human fear.Grave 75: What Archaeology FoundPień's cemetery does not appear on any historical maps. No records mention it. Its position outside the village — on a slope near a crossroads, far from any church or chapel — identifies it as what researchers describe as a "false cemetery," a burial ground for those the community had rejected or condemned. The study notes that such sites were used for "suicides, heretics, outsiders without municipal citizenship, vagrants, [and the] tragically deceased." The complete absence of Catholic religious paraphernalia across the site's 101 excavated graves has led researchers to suggest the population may have been Protestant — a further mark of marginality in the overwhelmingly Catholic Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of the 1600s.Grave 75 was discovered in August 2022. Alongside a complete skeleton, researchers found a sickle 36 cm (14.2 in) in length placed directly over the neck, its blade angled toward the throat; a triangular iron padlock fastened to the big toe of the left foot; and fragments of a decorative band woven from pure silver and gold threads running through fine silk. That textile — known as a galloon or galon — is a luxury object, accessible only to the wealthy or noble. Whatever this young woman was accused of, she was not a peasant.The sickle-and-padlock combination documented here has never before been recorded in a single grave in the published archaeological literature. Each object had independent meaning in Central European folk tradition: the sickle, a harvesting tool, carried protective power against supernatural forces and was positioned so that any attempt to rise would press the blade inward; the padlock was believed to "lock" the soul of a dangerous deceased person within the grave. Together they represent what the paper calls an attempt to "symbolically constrain the deceased's potential return to the world of the living.""It was unusual that there were two precautions, two methods of showing that this skeleton should be kept in the grave — so the fear of the body coming back to life was greater," Poliński said in news coverage of the study.What Ancient DNA and Isotopes RevealThe scientific core of the 2026 study is the application of methods that were not available when the site was first excavated, or when earlier "vampire burial" research at Poland's Drawsko cemetery used simpler strontium-isotope techniques to identify cholera epidemic victims in the 1700s.Mitochondrial DNA extracted from Zosia's remains placed her in haplogroup J1c2c1 — a West Eurasian lineage very rare among modern Slavic populations but whose ancestral nodes are found predominantly in ancient and modern Scandinavian samples. The researchers note that the topology of this haplogroup "might point to the Scandinavian origin of the entire haplogroup J1c2c1 and its further dispersals into different parts of Europe, presumably from the Viking period onward." That said, haplogroup assignment is probabilistic, and the study explicitly identifies Scandinavian ancestry as "one potential scenario."Strontium (87Sr/86Sr) and oxygen (δ18O) isotope analysis of her childhood teeth told a complementary story: the signatures fall within the range for the local Pień area, as well as for several other European regions including southern Scandinavia. The most coherent interpretation is that Zosia was born and grew up near Pień — but that her Scandinavian ancestry was several generations old, visible in her genes but not in her geography. In a small 17th-century village, family origins of that kind could be known. Or suspected.Carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis of her bones told a third story. Despite her silk-and-gold headband suggesting elite status, her levels place her among adults at the cemetery with low animal-protein consumption — indicating periods of malnutrition rather than consistent wealth. The hardships of the Little Ice Age, which placed the coldest and most disrupted decades of European climate directly over the 1620–1674 span of this burial, meant that even wealthy families in rural Poland faced periodic food scarcity.Her height is calculated from femoral length at 162 to 168 cm (approximately 5 ft 4 in to 5 ft 6 in), average for a woman of the period. Skeletal analysis also identified a hemangioma — a benign vascular tumor — in her sternum. The condition could have caused chest deformity visible to others, chronic pain, and in some presentations, episodes of fainting or altered consciousness. In a village with no medical framework for such symptoms, they would readily read as supernatural.What the Sickle Handle RevealsOne detail from the new analysis has received less attention than the DNA results: the composition of the sickle's wooden handle. Analysis of surviving organic material identified it as most likely birch, though alder or maple are also possible. Birch carried its own layer of symbolic meaning in Polish folk tradition — it was widely associated with protection against demons and witchcraft. If the choice of birch was intentional, it suggests the community was layering protective symbolism into the object itself, not simply placing any available tool across the woman's neck.The grave also appears to have been reopened while the body was still partially decomposing. Soil disturbance patterns and the position of one arm suggest the sickle was not placed at the original burial but added later — possibly, as oral tradition records, after a period of unexplained misfortune in the village. The padlock, found unlocked, had apparently been fastened to her toe at the original burial; the researchers believe it was discovered open when the grave was reopened, adding to the community's alarm."These people burying her did everything they could in order to prevent her from coming back from the dead," Swedish forensic sculptor Oscar Nilsson, who built the 2024 3D facial reconstruction, said, quoted in CBS News coverage. "We have done everything we can in order to bring her back to life."What Science Made of Her FaceIn 2024, Nilsson built Zosia's face from a 3D-printed replica of her skull, applying layers of plasticine clay muscle by muscle using published forensic tissue-depth data calibrated for estimated age, sex, ancestry, and body weight. DNA-informed estimates guided choices about eye, hair, and skin coloring. The process took hundreds of hours. The resulting reconstruction — a young woman with a neutral, watchful expression — was featured in the 2024 PBS Secrets of the Dead documentary Field of Vampires, which followed the Nicolaus Copernicus team through the project.Professor Poliński described first seeing the finished reconstruction as a "mind-blowing" moment. "He added so much feeling, so much emotion," Poliński said of Nilsson's work. "It wasn't a mask."Copper in the Mouth: Possible Third Restraint — or Something StrangerThe most disquieting finding in the 2026 study is what the researchers found on Zosia's palate, nasal cavity, and cervical vertebrae: a distinctive greenish stain, confirmed by elemental analysis (SEM-EDS and MAXRF) to carry a high copper signal. Coins in the mouth of the deceased were an established anti-vampiric or anti-demonic practice at both the Pień and Drawsko cemeteries — but the discoloration here is far larger than a coin would produce. The team ruled out a coin; they have not identified the object.What makes this detail particularly unsettling is the researchers' working hypothesis: they believe, per Phys.org's coverage, that a copper-containing object or medicinal substance was "deliberately pushed deep into her mouth or nasal passage around the time of her death." That phrase — around the time of her death — implies the copper object may not have been a purely post-mortem protective measure. The community may have attempted some form of intervention, possibly medical, possibly ritual, before or at the moment she died. If so, it complicates the simple narrative of a village acting only out of fear of a corpse, and suggests instead that the fear of Zosia may have been present while she was still alive.Further microtomographic examination of the triangular padlock is scheduled for October 2026 at the AGH University of Science Technology in Kraków, and may clarify details of its manufacture and origin.What Pień Tells Us About FearThe Pień cemetery is, by some measures, the most significant assemblage of anti-revenant burials yet documented in early modern Europe. Of 101 excavated 17th-century graves, at least a dozen show non-normative or restraint-related practices. A child aged five to seven was buried face-down with a triangular padlock near the feet — the same design as the one on Zosia's toe. Fear of the returning dead was not occasional or idiosyncratic at Pień. It was structural.John Blair, professor emeritus of medieval history and archaeology at the University of Oxford and not involved in the study, observed that females buried with sickles over their throats "were undoubtedly perceived as potentially dangerous corpses, that might harm the living if not disabled in this way," according to CNN.Scholars have long suggested that the typical profile of anti-revenant burial candidates included foreigners, the physically unusual, suicides, unbaptized infants, and heretics. Zosia's case complicates that profile. Her silk-and-gold accessories place her among the elite. Her isotope signature places her childhood locally. Yet she ended up in an outcast cemetery with three separate restraints. The researchers suggest her Scandinavian genetic ancestry — potentially known to the community through her family lineage — combined with her visible physical symptoms, her sudden and unexplained death, and a context of Little Ice Age hardship may have been enough to make her the designated source of misfortune.It is an old mechanism. In 17th-century Poland as in many other times and places, communities under extreme pressure needed an explanation for why people were dying and crops were failing. Someone had to be blamed. As the researchers write, anti-vampiric burial practice can be understood as any ritual action "not typical for a specific human group, cultural unit, or region" — a definition broad enough to encompass the enormous variety of protective measures documented across early modern Europe, and narrow enough to point directly at whoever the community most feared.What Comes Next at PieńThe 2026 paper is explicitly described as the first systematic, peer-reviewed multidisciplinary analysis of Grave 75. Earlier reporting — including the 2024 PBS documentary — drew on preliminary findings only. The AGH microtomography of the padlock, scheduled for October 2026, may reveal its manufacturing provenance and possibly its symbolic significance. Additional questions, including the cause of Zosia's death, remain open; the researchers say they are "getting closer" but further testing is required.Excavations at the Pień site are ongoing. The cemetery has been worked since 2005, and geophysical surveys have already identified anomalies that may indicate additional burials not yet reached. For the moment, Zosia remains the most fully studied individual at the site — restored, through science, to something approaching personhood: a young woman with a Scandinavian haplogroup, a silk cap, a sternal tumor, a childhood spent near this village, and a death so frightening to the people around her that they did not stop at one precaution, or even two.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat makes the Pień vampire burial different from other anti-vampire burials in Poland?The 2026 study documents three separate protective measures in a single grave — a padlock on the toe, a sickle placed over the neck when the grave was later reopened, and a copper object apparently inserted into the mouth around the time of death. No published archaeological record has previously documented the padlock-and-sickle combination in the same burial, let alone a third copper measure. The combination, along with ancient DNA tracing haplogroup J1c2c1 to Scandinavian ancestry and stable-isotope evidence of a locally raised individual, makes Grave 75 one of the most thoroughly analyzed anti-revenant burials in early modern European archaeology, according to the Poliński et al. study.What does haplogroup J1c2c1 mean, and does it prove Zosia was Scandinavian?Haplogroup J1c2c1 is a mitochondrial DNA lineage (inherited through the maternal line) whose ancestral nodes appear predominantly in ancient and modern Scandinavian populations. However, haplogroup assignment indicates probable ancestry, not individual birthplace. The study's stable-isotope analysis of Zosia's childhood teeth indicates she grew up in the Pień area — so her Scandinavian ancestry was almost certainly several generations removed by the time she was born. The researchers describe Scandinavian origin as "one potential scenario," not a proven fact, per the study.Why was a wealthy young woman buried in an outcast cemetery?The Pień cemetery was positioned outside the village at a crossroads, with no religious artifacts, on land not appearing on any historical maps — all indicators of what researchers call a "false cemetery" reserved for those society rejected, regardless of social status. Zosia's silk-and-gold galloon shows she was from an elite family, yet the study demonstrates that wealth offered no protection from supernatural accusation in 17th-century Poland. The researchers suggest her Scandinavian genetic background, her visible medical symptoms (including a chest hemangioma that could cause fainting), and a sudden unexplained death during the hardships of the Little Ice Age may collectively account for the fear her community felt, as reported by CNN.What was the copper object in her mouth, and could it have been medical?Elemental analysis (SEM-EDS and MAXRF) confirmed high copper content in staining on Zosia's palate, nasal cavity, and cervical vertebrae. The discoloration is too large to have come from a coin. The researchers believe a copper-containing object or substance was "deliberately pushed deep into her mouth or nasal passage around the time of her death," according to Phys.org. Photograph: Arif Kartono/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A policeman walks in front of buses in Kuala Lumpur carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia despite concerns for their safety in the war-torn country. Photograph: Arif Kartono/AFP/Getty Images Malaysia Malaysia begins Myanmar repatriations despite warnings from UN and rights groups Kuala Lumpur plans to send a total of 5,000 Myanmar nationals back to the war-torn country despite persecution concerns Agence France-Presse Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.05 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Malaysia began sending back about 1,500 Myanmar nationals on Tuesday, the government confirmed, as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants and asylum seekers by returning them to the war-torn country. The group is the first of 5,000 Myanmar citizens that Kuala Lumpur says agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres amid a huge uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia. Both the UN and advocacy organisations voiced concern on Tuesday, saying the group could face a dangerous homecoming in Myanmar, where a civil war has raged since 2021 . Exile has not broken young Rohingya people. But survival cost us more than our homes | Ajas Khan Read more Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have officially clarified the number of Rohingya people in the first group, and there is worry they may be returned to a country where they face persecution rights groups say amounts to genocide . The Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN. Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017. On Tuesday afternoon, AFP reporters saw three ships belonging to the Myanmar navy, used in a previous repatriation exercise, departing from Malaysia’s Lumut naval base. The Myanmar nationals were processed at the naval base before boarding dozens of buses which arrived under police escort at the Majlis Perbandaran Manjung stadium. Malaysia’s interior ministry confirmed that the repatriations were under way. View image in fullscreen A policeman walks in front of buses carrying Myanmar nationals being repatriated from Malaysia. Photograph: Arif Kartono/AFP/Getty Images It said it a statement that the repatriation was part of the government’s plan to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum-seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar. “This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said. But in Geneva, the UN rights chief, Volker Turk, urged Malaysia to stop the process immediately, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground. “This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses, and where many cruelly face the real risk of more of the same violence again upon their return,” he said in a statement. “The conditions are far from safe and sustainable, and it is deeply questionable whether any return in these circumstances can be considered truly voluntary. “The hundreds of thousands who have fled Myanmar in fear for their lives must be protected, and their fundamental human rights to seek asylum and protection abroad properly considered.” The Malaysian prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya. The plan was announced after authorities detained more than 100 Rohingya who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur. They were seeking help after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state. They were later released after officials confirmed they held valid UN documentation. Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups. Last week more than 160 civil society groups in a joint statement called upon the Malaysian government to “immediately halt the deportations,” pending talks with civil organisations about the situation on the ground in Myanmar. Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognise refugee status. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ly.text: Image source, Petko Momchilov / Reuters Image caption, Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment By Emer Moreau Published 6 October 2026 A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say. A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued. Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable". Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said. The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania. It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board. A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched. Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain. Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan. Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law". He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable." He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning. "Commercial ships â and innocent crews â are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning." "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable." Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea. A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media. On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/Shutterstock Retail industry Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week Business live – latest updates Mark Sweney Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.35 EDT First published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey , announces his budget next week. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall. The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic . While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East. In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict. Stripping out the increase from fuel, retail sales fell 0.7% in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City. “October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics. “This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in [the final quarter of this year and the first quarter of next]. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.” Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector. Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather. The only sector to record an increase in sales last month – apart from automotive fuel – was department stores, where the volume of goods bought rose 0.2%. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The fall in monthly sales follows a bumper August, with the ONS revising figures up from a 0.5% monthly rise to 0.7% . This helped fuel a 0.7% increase in sales over the three months to the end of September compared with the previous quarter. “Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel, which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East,” said Hannah Finselbach, a senior statistician at the ONS. “Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.” Explore more on these topics Retail industry Budget 2026 John Healey Budget Office for National Statistics Petrol prices UK cost of living crisis news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget Hobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer data Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn Asos says customers’ names, contact details and search histories hacked Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store to close in January Poundland management in talks to lead bid that could save 11,000 jobs Boss of Beaverbrooks urges government to give businesses ‘a bit of a break’ Flash sale: AO snaps up camera seller Jessops from Dragons’ Den star Peter Jones Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail
